content: The recommended treatment for tuberculosis (TB) in HIV-infected adults, when the causative organisms are known or presumed to be susceptible to first-line drugs, involves a 6-month regimen. Initial Phase (First 2 Months): The initial phase consists of isoniazid (INH), a rifamycin (e.g., rifampin or rifabutin), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB). Continuation Phase (Last 4 Months): The continuation phase includes isoniazid (INH) and a rifamycin. For patients with advanced HIV infection (CD4 counts <100/µL), daily or three-times-weekly therapy is recommended during both the initial and continuation phases. In patients with less advanced immunosuppression (CD4 counts ≥100/µL), twice-weekly therapy may be considered. However, once-weekly INH/rifapentine in the continuation phase is contraindicated in all HIV-infected patients due to an unacceptably high relapse rate, often with organisms that have acquired resistance to rifamycins. HIV-infected patients with advanced immunosuppression (CD4 counts <100/µL) treated with twice-weekly rifampinor rifabutin-based regimens have also shown a risk of developing acquired rifampin resistance. Therefore, these patients should receive daily or three-times-weekly treatment. Directly observed therapy (DOT) and other adherence-promoting strategies are particularly important for patients with HIV-related TB. The management of HIV-related TB is complex and requires expertise in treating both HIV and TB. Drug interactions between antituberculosis medications and antiretroviral agents, particularly rifamycins, are a significant concern. Rifampin can be used with certain combinations of antiretroviral agents, but rifabutin, which has fewer problematic drug interactions, may be used as an alternative. Rifabutin appears to be equally effective, though dose adjustments for both rifabutin and antiretroviral agents may be necessary. As new antiretroviral agents and pharmacokinetic data become available, these recommendations may be updated. HIV-infected patients receiving antituberculosis treatment may occasionally experience a temporary worsening of symptoms, signs, or radiographic findings of TB. This phenomenon, known as a paradoxical reaction, is thought to result from immune reconstitution due to effective antiretroviral therapy. Symptoms may include high fevers, lymphadenopathy, expanding central nervous system lesions, and worsening chest radiographic findings. A diagnosis of paradoxical reaction should only be made after thoroughly excluding other causes, particularly TB treatment failure. Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may provide symptomatic relief for paradoxical reactions. For severe cases, prednisone (1–2 mg/kg per day for 1–2 weeks, followed by a gradual taper) may be used, although there is no evidence from controlled trials to support this approach.
